answer:
Removing biases slightly reduces parameters, memory traffic, and operations, and simplifies some fused kernels. Large matrix weights dominate parameter count, so the savings are usually modest. A surrounding normalization may also make certain offsets redundant, but this depends on placement: RMSNorm does not subtract the mean and does not generally cancel an arbitrary bias. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467)

$$y=Wx+b,\qquad \Delta P=d_{out}\ \text{when the bias is removed}.$$

For a square $d\times d$ projection the removed fraction is about $1/d$, not a dramatic reduction. Bias-free training is an architectural choice validated by experiments, not a theorem that biases are useless. Some successful architectures retain biases or use special learned offsets. Inspect the model definition rather than generalizing “almost all layers” to every LLM. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00118) [4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)
